claim: Zionism is a colonial project that stole the land.

heard.who: Lorenzo Veracini, historian of settler colonialism, in a 2022 interview
heard.quote: Zionism is a settler colonial movement and Israel is a settler colonial state. This is not an insult; it is a statement of fact.

answer: Zionism's founding text, the Basel Program of 1897, says its aim is 'a home in Palestine secured by public law' for the Jewish people, to be reached partly by promoting Jewish settlement in Palestine by farmers and workers (the 1897 Jewish Chronicle translation says 'colonization', others 'settlement'). Herzl called the idea the restoration of the Jewish state. But Zionism was never one thing: political, labour, religious, cultural and revisionist Zionists differed, and bi-nationalists such as Brit Shalom wanted Jews and Arabs to share the country. Many Jews opposed it: the Bund, Reform rabbis, and the Orthodox Agudat Israel. Scholars disagree whether 'settler colonial' fits: Veracini says it does; Dowty says there was no mother country, though he also writes that early Zionists saw the Arabs as 'a major inconvenience'; Penslar says Israel is a settler colonial state toward the Palestinians but not only that.

facts.text: The first of the Basel Program's means was promoting Jewish settlement in Palestine by farmers and workers. The English translation printed in the Jewish Chronicle on 3 September 1897 (translator unknown; reprinted in the Posen Library and on the COJS page) renders it 'the promotion, on suitable lines, of the colonization of Palestine by Jewish agricultural and industrial workers'; the Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia render the same point 'settlement'. The Jewish Encyclopedia adds that the Second Congress took up 'the question of colonization' through a plan drawn up by a colonization committee, and the historian Derek Penslar notes that Herzl called the Zionist bank the Jewish Colonial Trust. The German original was not read, so this card does not say that 'colonization' was the word of the 1897 text itself.

facts.text: Some Zionists wanted a state shared by Jews and Arabs. Berit Shalom, founded in Jerusalem in 1925, proposed a bi-national solution with Jews and Arabs having an equal share in the administration regardless of their numbers; it never had more than 200 members. Martin Buber's philosophy influenced its members, and Judah Magnes advocated bi-nationalism but was never a member. The Marxist Ha-Shomer Ha-Tsair also defined a bi-national state of parity as its version of Zionism's aim.

facts.text: Scholars disagree, in their own words, on whether 'settler colonial' describes Zionism. The historian Lorenzo Veracini says 'Zionism is a settler colonial movement and Israel is a settler colonial state.' The political scientist Alan Dowty says there was 'no métropole, no mother country of which the settlers were an extension' and that most immigrants were refugees; but he also writes that 'the presence of another people was first and foremost a major inconvenience', which the early Zionists 'tried their best to ignore and minimalize', and that they did not recognise the Arabs 'as another people with their own collective claims'. The historian Derek Penslar says Israel 'is a settler colonial state in terms of its relationship with the palestinians who are dispossessed in 1948', also has a 'cult of postcolonial technological development', and that 'the settler colonial paradigm only explains so much'. The historian Rashid Khalidi says the early Zionists made no bones about doing it 'as part of a settler colonial process'.

contested.text: Position: Zionism is settler colonialism. Rashid Khalidi says the early Zionists used the language of colonisation themselves and that the movement took over land from Palestinians. Lorenzo Veracini says the lack of a single mother country shows only that Zionism was not 'colonial' in the imperial sense, not that it was not settler colonial; his interview draws on Patrick Wolfe's concept of a 'logic of elimination'. Wolfe's own general statement of the theory, quoted here, is that settler colonizers come to stay, so that invasion is a structure and not an event; his words on Zionism were not read.

contested.text: Position: the description does not fit. Alan Dowty, a political scientist, says classic colonialism needs a metropole, a mother country whose agents the colonists are, and that there was none; he adds that most Jews who came were refugees fleeing persecution and not agents of a sponsor. Supporters of the description answer that a settler movement needs no single mother country, and that historical ties to the land do not remove the question of the people already living there. Dowty also writes, in the same article, that the presence of another people was 'a major inconvenience' which the early Zionists tried to ignore, and that they did not recognise the Arabs as a people with collective claims; this is the part of his account that the other side cites. This card reports the argument; it does not decide it.

contested.text: Position: both frames are needed, and comparison is a tool, not a verdict. Derek Penslar, a Harvard historian of Zionism, said in his own words at a 2024 Harvard Divinity School event that Israel 'is a settler colonial state in terms of its relationship with the palestinians' but also has a postcolonial side, and that to call a country settler colonial 'means that there's a certain pattern of relations between newcomers and current residents', after which 'you have to start asking all kinds of other questions'.

Arnon Degani, in a peer-reviewed article (abstract on the Ben-Gurion University research portal), applies the settler-colonial framework to Zionism to explain two simultaneous trends in the same movement: aggressive ethnonationalism affecting Palestinians today, and a historical drive toward Jewish-Arab parity and integration.

could_not_verify: Jewish opposition to Zionism today: I found readable pages on the Haredi groups (Satmar, Neturei Karta) only; I did not find reliable readable pages on secular or liberal Jewish anti-Zionism today (for example Jewish Voice for Peace), which is advocacy at best.
Wolfe's own application of his theory to Zionism (his book Traces of History) was not readable; I quote only his general statement of the theory.

The German original of the Basel Program (the means clause, 'Besiedlung' or another word) was not on any page I could read; the card says whose English translation uses 'colonization' (the Jewish Chronicle's of 3 September 1897, translator unknown) and that two reference works say 'settlement'. A person would need the German text in the stenographic protocol of the First Zionist Congress (1898) or a library scan.

Penslar's own written work (his 2001 article 'Zionism, Colonialism and Postcolonialism' and the book Zionism: An Emotional State) was not readable here; his words on the card come from the transcript of a 2024 Harvard Divinity School event. Penslar's earlier Dartmouth and Zuckerman Sivan second-hand reports were dropped.

Herzl's own use of 'colony' and 'colonization' in his diaries and in The Jewish State: only Penslar's remark that Herzl called the bank the Jewish Colonial Trust was found, in an event transcript; no readable primary page.

Avalon's text of the Basel Program did not load; the quote is from the Posen Library, which prints the Jewish Chronicle's 1897 translation. Other translations differ in small ways ('public law', 'publicly and legally assured').

The card carries no fact on whether Zionism 'stole the land' (that belongs to the land card in this chapter) or on Arabs in the founding texts beyond Dowty's remark; a person would need Herzl's diaries and the Zionist Congress protocols.
not_claimed: This card does not decide whether 'settler colonialism' is the right label; it gives both sides.
It does not say Zionism was a single movement with a single aim, or that all Zionists sought a state shared with Arabs or a state alone.
It does not say the Basel Program ruled out an Arab presence; it is silent on the people already living there.
It does not claim the opposition to Zionism among Jews was only religious or only socialist; the sources named give three kinds.

skeptic.notes: Read 2+ sources for facts 0-6 and every contested entry. Veracini (heard) and Dowty are quoted accurately. [must-fix] Fact 1 said 'colonization' was the movement's own word. The pages show it is one translator's choice (COJS, Posen) while the Encyclopaedia Judaica and Jewish Encyclopedia say 'settlement', and the German was not read; the Posen quote did not even contain the word. Corrected in text and quote. The old answer's 'he and his successors used the word colonization' had no source and is removed. [must-fix] Old answer said 'Khalidi, Wolfe and Veracini say yes': no quote has Wolfe applying his theory to Zionism (the card admits it). Removed. Fact 5 rests on three claims each with one source (Bund; Reform rabbis; Agudat); fact 3 now has one reliable origin (Unpacked has no institution named, relabelled other; the other two quotes are one Encyclopaedia Judaica page); fact 4's JTA page was unreadable (404). [must-fix] Penslar (contested[2]) is known only through a student-paper report of a panel and a colleague's summary; the text now says so; his own words are needed. [should-fix] Fact 4: Magnes was never a Berit Shalom member (Encyclopaedia Judaica) and the card called him a supporter; fixed. Fact 5: the Reform resolution is a 1917 reaction to Balfour, later reversed; not on the card. Fact 6 and could_not_verify: only Haredi anti-Zionism is carried. Dowty's text that early Zionists treated the Arabs as 'a major inconvenience' to be ignored is omitted though it is in the cited article (the Palestinian side would cite it). [nit] 'Historian at Ben-Gurion University' for Degani is not on the portal page. 'heard' (Veracini) states the 'colonial' half; nothing here answers 'stole the land'. Strongest objections: Palestinian side, the card omits Dowty's own concession and says nothing on the Arabs of Palestine in the founding texts (not_claimed says so); Israeli side, none beyond Dowty's included case.

citer.notes: 4 answer sentences remain. The remaining answer no longer says anything on the 'colonial' label, which is the claim being tested.
